desc:
You are given an array nums of positive integers. In one move you pick two adjacent elements a and b, pay a * b, and replace the pair by the single value max(a, b) (so the smaller one disappears and the array becomes one element shorter). Repeat until only one element remains.

Return the minimum total amount you can pay.

Example: nums = [6, 2, 4] gives 32. Merge 2 and 4 first (cost 8, array becomes [6, 4]), then merge 6 and 4 (cost 24). Merging 6 and 2 first would cost 12 and leave [6, 4], for a total of 36, which is worse.
hints: Whenever two neighbours merge, the smaller of the two is removed for good. Its whole cost is its value times one other number. Which neighbour should it be multiplied with to be as cheap as possible?
A value that is smaller than both of its current neighbours should be removed by merging it with the smaller of those two neighbours. A good order is therefore to remove local minima first.
Scan left to right with a stack that is strictly decreasing. When a new value x arrives, pop every top m with m ≤ x: pay m * min(new top, x). At the end pay the products of the remaining neighbours.
editorial: Every move removes exactly one element, namely the smaller of the merged pair, and charges that element times the other element of the pair. The best you can hope for when removing an element m is to pair it with the smaller of its two current neighbours, since it is no larger than either of them when it is a local minimum. Greedy removal of the smallest remaining element, always paired with its cheaper neighbour, is optimal: an exchange argument shows that postponing a removal never makes the partner smaller.

A stack makes the greedy linear. Keep values strictly decreasing from bottom to top, with a huge sentinel at the bottom. For a new value x, while the top m is at most x, it has a bigger neighbour on both sides (the element below it and x), so remove it and pay m * min(below, x). Then push x. When the scan ends the stack is strictly decreasing, so the smallest element is on top and is removed against the element below it: pay the product of each remaining adjacent pair.
Every element is pushed and popped at most once: O(n) time and O(n) space. The answer is at most about 5000 * 100 * 100 = 5 * 10<sup>7</sup>, so it fits in 32 bits.
